newsitem.title: UK: British government denies coverup in E.coli report.
newsitem.headline: British government denies coverup in E.coli report.

text.p: The British government was plunged into a further controversy over food safety on Thursday when it was forced to deny it had suppressed a damaging report on unhealthy conditions in abattoirs.

Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg, already under fire for his handling of the mad cow crisis, told parliament that the document had been "redrafted", but had then been made available to meat industry officials.

The row broke after a copy of the draft of a report prepared by hygiene service officer Bill Swann in 1995 on the state of hygiene in each slaughterhouse in Britain was leaked to the Financial Times newspaper.

It found that animal faeces were finding their way onto carcasses being prepared for human consumption. Such faeces can harbour E.coli, an organism responsible for recent food poisoning outbreaks in Scotland in which 20 people died.
Swann told the Financial Times that if his recommendations were carried out uniformly in Britain's 600 slaughterhouses "the risk from E.coli...would be considerably diminished."
But in his statement to MPs, Hogg said: "It is said that important recommendations were not carried out. This is not so."
He said the first draft of Swann's report "was regarded as rather unsatisfactory, and not fully reflecting the views of others who had taken part in the review".
Swann was asked to rewrite his contribution but refused, so the job was done by a colleague and the "revised and condensed version" put to industry representatives last June, Hogg said.

He said the Conservative government's action in setting up a Meat Hygiene Service two years ago had led to "constantly improving" standards of inspection in abattoirs to ensure that only healthy carcasses were supplied to butchers.

The opposition Labour Party said it believed the government may have held the report back because its publication would have coincided with ministers' admission of a possible link between mad cow disease, or Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), and its human equivalent Creutzfeld-Jakob Disease (CJD).

The crisis over mad cow disease resulted in a European Union worldwide ban on British beef exports and crippled the British beef industry. It led to two widespread culling operations and cost the government 3.5 billion pounds ($5.7 billion).
"Why doesn't this government understand that when it comes to food safety matters, we have to be open and up front?" said Labour's agriculture spokesman Gavin Strang.
"Secrecy only has the effect of undermining consumer confidence in the safety of our food."

Professor Hugh Pennington, the scientist appointed by the government to look into the E.coli outbreak in Scotland, said he had not been told about the findings which could have helped him in his investigation.
"I'm a bit annoyed," he said. "It is an issue everybody knows we are looking at."
